title: Our hotfix took fifty six minutes to deploy because the depot screens never hung up
summary:
Our tracking API runs on eight EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, deployed in place by CodeDeploy one instance at a time. Each instance is taken out of the target group, updated, health checked and put back. On a quiet day a release took about eight minutes and nobody had ever timed it more carefully than that.

In October a carrier changed an error format, and every status update from them was failing to parse. The fix was two lines, reviewed in ten minutes and merged at 14:20. It finished deploying at 15:16. For that hour depots were ringing customer service about vans the system said had not left.

Almost all of the time was spent waiting. When CodeDeploy blocks traffic to an instance, the load balancer stops sending it new requests and waits for the requests already in flight to finish before it completes deregistration. It waits at most the target group's deregistration delay, which defaults to three hundred seconds. A target with nothing in flight is released at once, which is why our early releases had been quick.

By October they were not. In the summer we had added a live board for the depot offices: a page that holds a server-sent events stream open to the API and receives each van's position as it changes. Every depot screen kept one request open, all day, and the load balancer spread them across all eight instances. Every instance therefore had a request that would never finish on its own, and every deregistration waited the full five minutes. One instance at a time, that was forty minutes of waiting on top of the work itself. The board had been slowing every release for three months, and it took a hurry for us to notice.

The deregistration delay is now thirty seconds, longer than any ordinary request we serve. A BeforeBlockTraffic hook tells the application to close its event streams, and the board's EventSource reconnects by itself within a few seconds, to an instance that is staying. Releases run two instances at a time, and the pipeline reports how long each step took, so the number we watch is time from merge to the last instance serving.

A deploy is as slow as the longest request it is willing to wait for. Ours was willing to wait for a request designed never to end.

– Sergey Shinder

title: The last 20% of an AI-built app: nine things that actually block launch
summary:
I keep hearing the same story from people who built something real with Cursor, Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Replit: the app exists, the demo works, and it has been "almost ready" for two months.

The 20% they are missing is rarely a feature. It is a set of integration seams that a generator will happily write code around and never solve. Here are the nine that block launches most often, in the order I check them, with the symptom and the fix.

1. Sessions that only exist in memory

Symptom: you can log in, and a refresh logs you out. Or login works on localhost and not on the deployed domain.

What's happening: the auth code stores a token in a module-level variable, or sets a cookie without Secure / SameSite, or signs with a secret regenerated on each cold start because it is generated at boot instead of read from the environment.

Fix: persist the session in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookie (or a refresh token in storage for mobile), keep SESSION_SECRET in the environment, and test after a hard reload, a tab restore and a cold start.

2. Auth that trusts the client

Symptom: everything works, and any user can read another user's records by changing an id.

What's happening: the generated code checks if (user) in the UI and never checks ownership on the server. With a hosted database, the row-level rules were never written at all.

Fix: every read and write on the server (or in the database rules) must be scoped to the authenticated subject. Not WHERE id = $1 but WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $subject. On Postgres with row-level security, the policy is the product; test it with two accounts, not one.

3. Payments that only pass in test mode

Symptom: Stripe checkout redirects and returns, but the order never appears, or appears twice, or appears in test mode and not in live mode.

What's happening: the success page is treated as proof of payment. No webhook, no signature verification, no idempotency key.

Fix: the redirect page is for the user, not for the database. Grant access in a webhook handler that verifies the signature against the raw body, and write the event id before doing anything else so a retried delivery cannot double-credit. Test with the Stripe CLI, then in live mode with a real card and a real refund.

4. Environment variables that only exist on your machine

Symptom: the deploy builds, then the first request that touches a third-party API returns 401 or undefined.

What's happening: .env is not committed (good), the platform's environment is empty (bad), and the code fails at the first network call instead of at boot.

Fix: validate the environment at startup and crash loudly if something is missing. Keep a .env.example in the repo. Treat "works locally" as unverified until it works on the deployed URL.

5. Database schema without migrations

Symptom: you changed a column two weeks ago and the deployed database does not have it. Nobody knows what the live schema is.

What's happening: the schema was applied by hand, or by a generator that ran once.

Fix: one source of truth, applied by a migration tool and run automatically on deploy. Seed data separate from schema. This is also the step that makes a staging environment possible at all.

6. CORS, cookies and the domain triangle

Symptom: the API works from localhost:3000 and fails from https://app.yourdomain.com with a CORS error or a dropped cookie.

What's happening: the API allows *, and a wildcard origin cannot carry credentials. Or the cookie was set on the API's host while the front end lives on another.

Fix: allow-list exact origins, send credentials: "include" from the client, return Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true plus an explicit origin from the server, and put front end and API on the same registrable domain when you can.

7. A deploy that is not a deploy

Symptom: the preview URL works, the custom domain shows an old build, www and the apex behave differently, and half the traffic is HTTP.

What's happening: DNS records were added once and never verified, the platform is serving a cached build, and SSL was issued for one hostname only.

Fix: decide the canonical host, redirect everything else to it, force HTTPS, verify both apex and www, and check a hard reload on a phone on cellular data — not just your laptop on the same network.

8. No error visibility

Symptom: a user says "it broke". You have nothing. No stack trace, no request, no timestamp.

What's happening: generated code has console.log and no error boundary, no server logging, no alert.

Fix: a client error boundary that reports, server logging with request ids, and one alert channel you actually read. You cannot operate what you cannot see, and operating is the difference between a demo and a product.

9. Mobile reality

Symptom: fine in a desktop browser, broken on a phone: the keyboard covers the input, fixed footers overlap content, 100vh is wrong, tap targets are 12px tall.

What's happening: layout was never checked on a device. 100vh was used instead of dynamic viewport units, and safe areas were ignored.

Fix: test on a real phone with the keyboard open. Use dvh, env(safe-area-inset-*), and touch targets of at least 44px. Then test a slow connection, because your users are not on your Wi-Fi.

If the product is a mobile app, add a tenth

Store review is its own integration seam: privacy manifest, permission strings, a real account-deletion path, and a build that does not depend on a debug keystore. Most rejections I see are not about the product at all.

Why generated code stalls exactly here

A generator is excellent at the parts that are visible in a single file and weak at the parts that span files, environments and time: secrets, webhooks, migrations, domains, ownership checks. None of those are hard individually. All of them are invisible until you try to ship, and each one looks like "just one more bug".

That is why the honest answer to "how long until launch?" is not a feature list. It is a checklist of seams, each verified in the environment it will actually run in.

What to do about it

If you are the builder, work the list in this order and stop adding features until it is empty. Authorization first, because it is the only item that can hurt a real user. Then payments in live mode. Then environment, migrations, domain, error visibility, mobile. Seven afternoons, and the app is a product.

If you would rather not spend those afternoons: I run a one-person studio that takes over half-finished AI-built codebases as they are, runs this checklist as a free review, and finishes the blockers through deploy and store release — usually in three to five days.

title: IP geolocation accuracy: why databases disagree on your IP
summary:
Originally published on proxymint.

IP geolocation accuracy by level, why two databases put one IP in different cities, how geofeeds work, and how to check a proxy exit's location yourself.

TL;DR

  • Trust the country, be careful with the city. MaxMind puts its own country accuracy at 99.8% but only 66% for US cities within 50 km (checked October 2026), so a city label that is off by one suburb is normal, not a bug.
  • Two lookup sites, two cities is the usual case. Each database mixes registry records, operator geofeeds, latency probes and its own data, and stores ranges of different sizes, so they split at city level all the time.
  • Mobile is the weak spot. A 2026 study of four providers found median mobile errors of 179-207 km, so an empty city on a carrier address is expected, and region is the level worth reading.
  • The target's database is the one that counts. If the exit is right and the page is still wrong, check DNS first: plain socks5:// resolves on your machine, which is the annoying one to spot.

Key takeaways

  • Read accuracy_radius, not just city.name. A city with a 500 km radius is a region guess, and code that ignores the radius throws the warning away.
  • Run the two-database check on your own exits. Look up 200 exits in an echo service and a local GeoLite2 file, and count country, region and city agreement before you scale a geo job.
  • Fix DNS before you blame the database. Use an http:// or socks5h:// proxy URL so the target name resolves on the proxy side, then set browser language and time zone for the market.
  • Target the level the page varies by. National prices need only country; local search and store pages need city, checked against the exact page you are collecting.

Read the full guide on proxymint, with the commands, tables and sources.

title: OpenTelemetry Collector to Loki Without Losing Trace Context
summary:
Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud

The scenario

A checkout request fails, you find the error in Grafana, and the log line has no trace link. The trace exists in Tempo, but nothing connects the two, so you copy IDs by hand. This is a common outcome when you ship logs from the OpenTelemetry Collector to Loki through a path that flattens the log record into a plain string and drops its trace fields.

The timing is good for a cleanup. Grafana 13.3 is the current release cycle (October 2026). Read its what's new page before you upgrade, because log and trace correlation lives in the Loki data source and Explore. The configuration below uses documented provisioning fields, not features specific to 13.3.

Short answer: use Loki's native OTLP endpoint (/otlp) with the Collector's otlphttp exporter, not the deprecated loki exporter, which has been removed from current contrib builds. Keep trace_id and span_id as structured metadata, never as labels. Then add a derived field in the Loki data source that points at Tempo. This applies when you run Loki 3.x and want one pipeline for logs, metrics and traces. It does not pay off if you only grep logs and never open traces.

Prerequisites

Check these before you change anything:

  • Loki 3.x with a TSDB index and schema v13. Loki keeps trace IDs in structured metadata, and structured metadata requires both. Verify your schema_config and the allow_structured_metadata limit in the Loki OTLP documentation.
  • An OpenTelemetry Collector contrib distribution. The filelog receiver and k8sattributes processor ship in contrib, not in the minimal core build. See the Collector docs.
  • A Tempo data source in Grafana (13.3.x here) and applications that already emit traces.
  • Network access from the Collector to Loki, for example a loki Service on port 3100. If Loki is multi-tenant, you also need the tenant ID.

Accept one cost up front: structured metadata adds storage and query-time work per log line. For high-volume debug logs, sample or filter them in the Collector before they reach Loki.

Step 1: Preserve trace context at the source

Trace context survives only if it reaches the Collector as fields on the log record, not as text inside the body. There are two paths.

Path A (preferred): the application uses an OpenTelemetry SDK log bridge or appender and sends OTLP to the Collector. When a log is emitted inside an active span, the SDK attaches that span's trace and span IDs to the record. You change nothing in the pipeline.

Path B: the application writes JSON lines to stdout that include trace_id and span_id, and the Collector tails the files. The Collector then has to promote those values into the record's real trace fields. The trace_parser operator in the filelog receiver does that. Without it, the IDs stay as ordinary attributes and the correlation features never see them.

Watch the ID formats. The documented expectation is a 32-hex-character trace ID and a 16-hex-character span ID. If your logger prints a different format, the parser cannot turn it into a valid trace context, so normalize it in the application's logger.

Step 2: Configure the Collector pipeline

This config covers both paths: OTLP in, plus Kubernetes container logs with trace parsing. It exports to Loki over native OTLP. Adjust paths, namespaces and the Loki address to your environment.

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317     # recent releases default to localhost only
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
  filelog:
    include: [/var/log/pods/*/*/*.log]
    # exclude the Collector's own pods to avoid a feedback loop, e.g.:
    # exclude: [/var/log/pods/observability_otel-collector-*/*/*.log]
    include_file_path: true
    operators:
      - type: container            # parses the CRI/containerd line format
      - type: json_parser          # only for JSON bodies
        parse_from: body
        if: 'body matches "^\\{"'
      - type: trace_parser         # promotes IDs into real trace fields
        trace_id:
          parse_from: attributes.trace_id
        span_id:
          parse_from: attributes.span_id

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
  k8sattributes: {}                # adds k8s.namespace.name, k8s.pod.name, ...
  batch: {}

exporters:
  otlphttp/loki:
    endpoint: http://loki:3100/otlp   # the exporter appends /v1/logs itself
    # headers:
    #   X-Scope-OrgID: team-a         # only if auth_enabled: true in Loki

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp, filelog]
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/loki]

Gotcha: do not append /v1/logs to the endpoint. The exporter adds it, and a doubled path produces 404 errors that look like a Loki outage. Keep batch after memory_limiter and k8sattributes so you batch the final, enriched records. Binding to 0.0.0.0 exposes the receivers on the pod network, so restrict access with a NetworkPolicy if needed.

The container operator and its options have changed across Collector releases. Confirm the field names against the filelog receiver README for the version you deploy.

Step 3: Decide what becomes a label

Loki's OTLP ingestion converts a documented default list of resource attributes into index labels, such as service.name, k8s.namespace.name and k8s.pod.name. Dots become underscores, so you query service_name. Everything else, including trace_id and span_id, is stored as structured metadata. That is the behavior you want.

Avoid the cardinality trap: never promote trace_id to a label. Every request would create a new stream, and Loki's performance and cost would degrade quickly. If you need different index labels than the defaults, set them on the Loki side. ignore_defaults: true makes your list replace the defaults instead of adding to them:

# loki.yaml (excerpt)
limits_config:
  allow_structured_metadata: true     # required for trace_id/span_id storage
  otlp_config:
    resource_attributes:
      ignore_defaults: true           # use only the list below as index labels
      attributes_config:
        - action: index_label         # keep this list short and low-cardinality
          attributes:
            - service.name
            - k8s.namespace.name

Check the exact key layout against the Loki version you run, because otlp_config options are version-dependent.

Step 4: Link logs to traces in Grafana

Provision a derived field on the Loki data source so each log line with a trace ID gets a link into Tempo. Provisioning from files keeps this reviewable, and the same idea applies to any other dashboards-as-code setup you keep in Git.

# provisioning/datasources/loki.yaml
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Loki
    type: loki
    uid: loki
    url: http://loki:3100
    jsonData:
      derivedFields:
        - name: TraceID
          matcherType: label          # read from structured metadata, not a regex on the line
          matcherRegex: trace_id
          url: '$${__value.raw}'      # $$ escapes env expansion in provisioning files
          datasourceUid: tempo        # UID of your Tempo data source

If your Grafana version does not offer matcherType: label, fall back to a regex derived field that matches the ID in the line. Check the Loki data source docs for the supported options.

On the Tempo side, a "logs for this span" link needs the Loki data source configured under Tempo's trace-to-logs settings. Keep the filter on service_name and k8s_namespace_name, and avoid tag mappings that don't exist in your labels.

Verify and test

First, send a synthetic OTLP log with a known trace ID straight to the Collector's HTTP port:

curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:4318/v1/logs \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"resourceLogs":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"otlp-smoke"}}]},
  "scopeLogs":[{"logRecords":[{"timeUnixNano":"'"$(date +%s)"'000000000",
  "severityText":"ERROR","body":{"stringValue":"smoke test"},
  "traceId":"5b8efff798038103d269b633813fc60c","spanId":"eee19b7ec3c1b174"}]}]}]}'

# then query Loki: label for the stream, structured metadata filter for the ID
# add --org-id= if Loki runs with auth_enabled: true
logcli query --addr=http://loki:3100 \
  '{service_name="otlp-smoke"} | trace_id="5b8efff798038103d269b633813fc60c"' --since=10m

A healthy result is one log line returned for that filter. A bare 200 from the Collector only means it accepted the record, so the Loki query is the real check. In Grafana Explore, the same line should show trace_id under structured metadata and a TraceID link that opens Tempo.

Next, watch the Collector's own metrics:

  • otelcol_exporter_sent_log_records should climb.
  • otelcol_exporter_send_failed_log_records should stay flat.

Recent Collector versions expose these with a _total suffix on the Prometheus endpoint, and names can differ by version. Confirm them on the Collector's internal telemetry endpoint.

If lines arrive but links are missing, check these in order:

  1. The log record had a trace ID when it left the Collector. Path B usually fails here.
  2. allow_structured_metadata is on.
  3. The derived field points at the right Tempo UID.

Where this leaves you

The reliable pattern has four parts: native OTLP into Loki, trace and span IDs kept as structured metadata, a short list of low-cardinality labels, and one derived field into Tempo. Do not adopt it if your logs are unstructured and uninstrumented. There is no trace context to preserve, and the extra storage buys you nothing. Start with one service on Path A, confirm the smoke test above, and only then roll the filelog pipeline out cluster-wide.

A checkout request fails, you find the error in Grafana, and the log line has no trace link. The trace exists in Tempo, but nothing connects the two, so you copy IDs by hand. This is a common outcome when you ship logs from the OpenTelemetry Collector to Loki through a path that flattens the log record into a plain string and drops its trace fields.

The timing is good for a cleanup. Grafana 13.3 is the current release cycle (October 2026). Read its what's new page before you upgrade, because log and trace correlation lives in the Loki data source and Explore. The configuration below uses documented provisioning fields, not features specific to 13.3.

Short answer: use Loki's native OTLP endpoint (/otlp) with the Collector's otlphttp exporter, not the deprecated loki exporter, which has been removed from current contrib builds. Keep trace_id and span_id as structured metadata, never as labels. Then add a derived field in the Loki data source that points at Tempo. This applies when you run Loki 3.x and want one pipeline for logs, metrics and traces. It does not pay off if you only grep logs and never open traces.

Prerequisites

Check these before you change anything:

  • Loki 3.x with a TSDB index and schema v13. Loki keeps trace IDs in structured metadata, and structured metadata requires both. Verify your schema_config and the allow_structured_metadata limit in the Loki OTLP documentation.
  • An OpenTelemetry Collector contrib distribution. The filelog receiver and k8sattributes processor ship in contrib, not in the minimal core build. See the Collector docs.
  • A Tempo data source in Grafana (13.3.x here) and applications that already emit traces.
  • Network access from the Collector to Loki, for example a loki Service on port 3100. If Loki is multi-tenant, you also need the tenant ID.

Accept one cost up front: structured metadata adds storage and query-time work per log line. For high-volume debug logs, sample or filter them in the Collector before they reach Loki.

Step 1: Preserve trace context at the source

Trace context survives only if it reaches the Collector as fields on the log record, not as text inside the body. There are two paths.

Path A (preferred): the application uses an OpenTelemetry SDK log bridge or appender and sends OTLP to the Collector. When a log is emitted inside an active span, the SDK attaches that span's trace and span IDs to the record. You change nothing in the pipeline.

Path B: the application writes JSON lines to stdout that include trace_id and span_id, and the Collector tails the files. The Collector then has to promote those values into the record's real trace fields. The trace_parser operator in the filelog receiver does that. Without it, the IDs stay as ordinary attributes and the correlation features never see them.

Watch the ID formats. The documented expectation is a 32-hex-character trace ID and a 16-hex-character span ID. If your logger prints a different format, the parser cannot turn it into a valid trace context, so normalize it in the application's logger.

Step 2: Configure the Collector pipeline

This config covers both paths: OTLP in, plus Kubernetes container logs with trace parsing. It exports to Loki over native OTLP. Adjust paths, namespaces and the Loki address to your environment.

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317     # recent releases default to localhost only
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
  filelog:
    include: [/var/log/pods/*/*/*.log]
    # exclude the Collector's own pods to avoid a feedback loop, e.g.:
    # exclude: [/var/log/pods/observability_otel-collector-*/*/*.log]
    include_file_path: true
    operators:
      - type: container            # parses the CRI/containerd line format
      - type: json_parser          # only for JSON bodies
        parse_from: body
        if: 'body matches "^\\{"'
      - type: trace_parser         # promotes IDs into real trace fields
        trace_id:
          parse_from: attributes.trace_id
        span_id:
          parse_from: attributes.span_id

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
  k8sattributes: {}                # adds k8s.namespace.name, k8s.pod.name, ...
  batch: {}

exporters:
  otlphttp/loki:
    endpoint: http://loki:3100/otlp   # the exporter appends /v1/logs itself
    # headers:
    #   X-Scope-OrgID: team-a         # only if auth_enabled: true in Loki

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp, filelog]
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/loki]

Gotcha: do not append /v1/logs to the endpoint. The exporter adds it, and a doubled path produces 404 errors that look like a Loki outage. Keep batch after memory_limiter and k8sattributes so you batch the final, enriched records. Binding to 0.0.0.0 exposes the receivers on the pod network, so restrict access with a NetworkPolicy if needed.

The container operator and its options have changed across Collector releases. Confirm the field names against the filelog receiver README for the version you deploy.

Step 3: Decide what becomes a label

Loki's OTLP ingestion converts a documented default list of resource attributes into index labels, such as service.name, k8s.namespace.name and k8s.pod.name. Dots become underscores, so you query service_name. Everything else, including trace_id and span_id, is stored as structured metadata. That is the behavior you want.

Avoid the cardinality trap: never promote trace_id to a label. Every request would create a new stream, and Loki's performance and cost would degrade quickly. If you need different index labels than the defaults, set them on the Loki side. ignore_defaults: true makes your list replace the defaults instead of adding to them:

# loki.yaml (excerpt)
limits_config:
  allow_structured_metadata: true     # required for trace_id/span_id storage
  otlp_config:
    resource_attributes:
      ignore_defaults: true           # use only the list below as index labels
      attributes_config:
        - action: index_label         # keep this list short and low-cardinality
          attributes:
            - service.name
            - k8s.namespace.name

Check the exact key layout against the Loki version you run, because otlp_config options are version-dependent.

Step 4: Link logs to traces in Grafana

Provision a derived field on the Loki data source so each log line with a trace ID gets a link into Tempo. Provisioning from files keeps this reviewable, and the same idea applies to any other dashboards-as-code setup you keep in Git.

# provisioning/datasources/loki.yaml
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Loki
    type: loki
    uid: loki
    url: http://loki:3100
    jsonData:
      derivedFields:
        - name: TraceID
          matcherType: label          # read from structured metadata, not a regex on the line
          matcherRegex: trace_id
          url: '$${__value.raw}'      # $$ escapes env expansion in provisioning files
          datasourceUid: tempo        # UID of your Tempo data source

If your Grafana version does not offer matcherType: label, fall back to a regex derived field that matches the ID in the line. Check the Loki data source docs for the supported options.

On the Tempo side, a "logs for this span" link needs the Loki data source configured under Tempo's trace-to-logs settings. Keep the filter on service_name and k8s_namespace_name, and avoid tag mappings that don't exist in your labels.

Verify and test

First, send a synthetic OTLP log with a known trace ID straight to the Collector's HTTP port:

curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:4318/v1/logs \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"resourceLogs":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"otlp-smoke"}}]},
  "scopeLogs":[{"logRecords":[{"timeUnixNano":"'"$(date +%s)"'000000000",
  "severityText":"ERROR","body":{"stringValue":"smoke test"},
  "traceId":"5b8efff798038103d269b633813fc60c","spanId":"eee19b7ec3c1b174"}]}]}]}'

# then query Loki: label for the stream, structured metadata filter for the ID
# add --org-id= if Loki runs with auth_enabled: true
logcli query --addr=http://loki:3100 \
  '{service_name="otlp-smoke"} | trace_id="5b8efff798038103d269b633813fc60c"' --since=10m

A healthy result is one log line returned for that filter. A bare 200 from the Collector only means it accepted the record, so the Loki query is the real check. In Grafana Explore, the same line should show trace_id under structured metadata and a TraceID link that opens Tempo.

Next, watch the Collector's own metrics:

  • otelcol_exporter_sent_log_records should climb.
  • otelcol_exporter_send_failed_log_records should stay flat.

Recent Collector versions expose these with a _total suffix on the Prometheus endpoint, and names can differ by version. Confirm them on the Collector's internal telemetry endpoint.

If lines arrive but links are missing, check these in order:

  1. The log record had a trace ID when it left the Collector. Path B usually fails here.
  2. allow_structured_metadata is on.
  3. The derived field points at the right Tempo UID.

Where this leaves you

The reliable pattern has four parts: native OTLP into Loki, trace and span IDs kept as structured metadata, a short list of low-cardinality labels, and one derived field into Tempo. Do not adopt it if your logs are unstructured and uninstrumented. There is no trace context to preserve, and the extra storage buys you nothing. Start with one service on Path A, confirm the smoke test above, and only then roll the filelog pipeline out cluster-wide.

Related

  • AWS Cost Anomaly Alerts: Route to Owners with Tag Context
  • PostgreSQL 18 Asynchronous I/O: Settings Worth Testing

title: Cloud iOS Signing: A New Certificate on Every Build, and the Fix
summary:
Our iPhone builds run in the cloud, because we develop on Windows. The first working pipeline signed the app automatically and it worked, until it did not. Every run quietly created one more certificate in the developer account, and one day the builds started failing with a missing private key. This is what was happening and the setup that replaced it.

The symptom: certificates piling up

With cloud-managed signing during the archive step, the build asks the App Store Connect API for what it needs. In our case that meant a new Apple Development certificate with the note Created via API on every single build. They add up fast. The account has a limit on how many certificates of a type it can hold, which we hit at around eleven.

Then the second failure appeared: the archive step complained that the private key was not installed. A certificate without the matching private key on the machine is useless, and a fresh build machine never has the key of a certificate that an earlier machine created.

The tempting shortcut that fails later

The obvious idea is to archive without signing and sign when exporting. The archive succeeds, the export even produces a package, and the upload is rejected by App Store Connect with an invalid signature error, number 90035. The reason is that the frameworks embedded in the app stay unsigned when the archive was built with code signing switched off. Signing only the outer app is not enough, every embedded framework needs its own signature.

So there is no shortcut here. The archive has to be signed properly, with a certificate whose private key is present on the build machine.

The stable setup: one distribution key you keep

The fix is to stop letting every build invent its own identity. You create one distribution certificate, keep its private key safe outside the cloud service, and give the build the same key every time. The build then asks the API for the certificate and the provisioning profile, and the API returns the same certificate it already has for that key instead of minting a new one.

In our pipeline the private key is stored base64 encoded in a secret variable group, next to the App Store Connect API key and its two identifiers. During the build it is decoded to a file and checked with openssl, so a damaged secret fails in the first minute and not at the end of a long build.

The steps, in order

  • Rebuild the API key file as a clean PEM: secrets often arrive with their line breaks mangled, so strip the header and footer, whitespace and literal backslash-n sequences, then wrap the body at 64 characters and verify it with openssl.
  • Set the build number in the project and in the Info.plist, and print it again from the finished package before uploading.
  • Decode the distribution private key from the secret and check it with openssl.
  • Initialize the keychain on the build machine.
  • Fetch the signing files for the bundle id with the create flag, type iOS App Store. The tool reuses the certificate that belongs to your key.
  • Add the certificates to the keychain, then apply the provisioning profiles to the Xcode project.
  • Build the signed ipa from the project and scheme, then publish it to TestFlight.

Saving minutes

Build minutes on a macOS machine are limited on a free plan, and every failed signing run burns some of them. Two habits help. First, start the signing workflow only by hand, so a push does not spend minutes. Second, keep a separate simulator workflow that builds without signing and never talks to Apple. It finds ordinary compile errors quickly and for free in terms of certificates.

We also run a script on Windows before any cloud build that checks the project for the mistakes we already paid for once. A rule that costs one second beats a build that costs ten minutes.

What to take away

  • Automatic cloud signing is fine for a first experiment, but it creates a new certificate per run.
  • An unsigned archive signed at export leaves frameworks unsigned and fails upload validation.
  • Create one distribution certificate, keep its private key backed up, and pass it to every build as a secret.
  • Validate secrets early in the build, and print the version numbers from the final package.

FAQ

Why did the builds fail with a missing private key?

Each run created a new certificate on a new machine, and the private key of a certificate exists only on the machine that created it.

Can I archive without signing and sign later?

Not reliably. The embedded frameworks stay unsigned and App Store Connect rejects the upload with an invalid signature error.

Where should the distribution private key live?

In a secure backup you control, and in the CI service as a secret variable, never in the repository.

Do I need a Mac to set this up?

No. The certificate request and the key can be created on any machine, and the cloud build does the rest.

title: We moved our roles to include_role and the emergency certificate run skipped every task
summary:
Our integration gateways are eleven Linux servers holding the client certificates our carriers issue us. A role called partner_certs puts them in place, and its tasks are tagged certs, so when a carrier sends a renewal we can push just that with ansible-playbook site.yml --tags certs. That takes two minutes. The whole playbook takes forty.

In August we changed site.yml to load roles with include_role instead of the roles list, so each gateway could pick its roles from inventory in a loop. A full run behaved exactly as before, which is how we tested it.

In October a carrier certificate was due to expire at midnight. The new one arrived at four in the afternoon. An engineer ran the playbook with --tags certs and it finished green in under a minute: fact gathering ok, nothing changed, nothing failed. He assumed an earlier run had already put the files in place. At midnight every label request to that carrier started failing its TLS handshake.

Tags work differently for imports and includes. import_role is static: Ansible reads the role's tasks while it parses the playbook, so tags on those tasks are visible to --tags. include_role is dynamic: the role is loaded only when the include task itself runs, and under a tag filter that include is just another task that has to match. Ours had no tags. Ansible skipped it, never opened the role, and never saw a single task tagged certs. Tasks skipped by a tag filter are not even listed in the output, so the run looked like one with nothing to do.

We copied the certificate by hand at twenty past twelve. Each include task now carries its role's tags and passes them inward with apply, so the tasks inside inherit them. The wrapper we use for tagged runs counts the tasks that actually executed and fails if a tag selected none, because a targeted run that touched nothing is never what anybody meant.

A tag filter only looks at the tasks it can see. After the change, it could no longer see inside our roles.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Deploying Industrial Edge Applications across Multiple Sites
summary:
An industrial edge pilot can work perfectly while remaining difficult to reproduce.

The engineer knows which register requires scaling, which alarm is disabled and where the site-specific settings live. Deploying the same application elsewhere requires reconstructing those decisions.

A repeatable industrial edge deployment separates application logic from site configuration, node identity and runtime data. It also defines how each installation is validated, updated and recovered.

This guide explains the architecture and deployment practices behind that separation.

1. Define What Runs on the Node

An edge application may handle equipment acquisition, protocol conversion, local rules, operator screens, historical storage and upstream integration.

Document which functions belong locally and which depend on central services.

For each function, identify:

  • Required inputs.
  • External dependencies.
  • Expected behavior during disconnection.
  • Recovery behavior.
  • Resource requirements.

A local dashboard can still depend on remote authentication. A rule can still require a central API. Hosting software on site does not remove those dependencies automatically.

Keep safety functions and time-critical control within their engineered and validated implementations.

For background on acquisition, supervisory functions and deployment boundaries, see Iotellect’s SCADA architecture guide.

2. Separate the Deployment into Four Parts

Avoid copying an entire working installation to create another node.

Separate:

Application release: Reusable rules, screens, mappings and integration logic.

Site configuration: Equipment addresses, asset relationships and approved operating parameters.

Node identity and credentials: Unique identifiers and authorized connections.

Runtime data: History, events, operator actions and queued observations.

These categories need different handling.

An application update should not overwrite local history. A new installation should not inherit another node’s credentials. A rollback must account for persistent data and configuration compatibility.

3. Validate Site Configuration before Activation

Represent site differences as configuration rather than editing application logic at every location.

An illustrative configuration might look like this:

siteId: pumping-station-014
applicationVersion: 1.8.0
configurationVersion: 12

equipment:
  - assetId: pump-01
    deviceProfile: drive-profile-v3
    connection:
      protocol: modbus_tcp
      host: 192.0.2.10
      port: 502
      unitId: 1

telemetry:
  acquisitionIntervalMs: 2000
  staleAfterMs: 10000

storage:
  maximumQueueBytes: 4000000000

This is an application example, not an Iotellect configuration format.

Validation should check required fields, allowed values, supported device profiles and application compatibility.

A simplified validator could include:

def validate_config(config, release):
    require_nonempty(config.site_id)

    if config.application_version != release.version:
        raise ConfigurationError("Application version mismatch")

    if config.telemetry.stale_after_ms <= 0:
        raise ConfigurationError("Invalid freshness policy")

    for asset in config.equipment:
        if asset.device_profile not in release.supported_profiles:
            raise ConfigurationError("Unsupported device profile")

    return config

Production validation also needs schema checks, permitted operating ranges and appropriate error reporting.

Keep secrets out of ordinary exports. Use references to an appropriate credential-management mechanism.

4. Use Device Profiles to Normalize Equipment

Different equipment can expose the same operational concept through different representations.

One drive may report temperature as an integer requiring scaling. Another may expose a floating-point value.

A profile can map both into a shared measurement:

Source address
→ Data type
→ Scaling
→ Engineering unit
→ Application measurement

Document each profile’s:

  • Supported equipment and revisions.
  • Acquisition behavior.
  • Status mappings.
  • Timestamp origin.
  • Quality handling.
  • Available commands.
  • Confirmation method.

Test profiles against representative equipment. Protocol compatibility alone does not establish that the mapping is correct.

Preserve Observation Context

An application record might contain:

{
  "siteId": "pumping-station-014",
  "assetId": "pump-01",
  "measurement": "motor_temperature",
  "value": 61.7,
  "unit": "degC",
  "sourceTimestamp": "2026-11-18T08:30:00Z",
  "quality": "good",
  "profileVersion": "drive-profile-v3"
}

Preserve acquisition time separately from arrival time. An older observation may belong in history without replacing newer current state.

For platform-specific background, see the documentation on Data Table Timestamps and Quality.

5. Size Hardware against a Representative Workload

Tag count alone is insufficient for sizing an edge node.

Resource consumption also depends on acquisition frequency, protocol behavior, storage, calculations, operator sessions and recovery traffic.

Measure:

  • CPU and memory during normal operation.
  • Storage growth.
  • Dashboard response.
  • Queue growth during an outage.
  • Resource use during replay.
  • Application startup and recovery time.

Estimate raw storage using:

records per second
× average record size
× retention duration

For 50 records per second averaging 200 bytes:

50 × 200 × 86,400
= 864,000,000 bytes per day

That is approximately 864 MB per day, before indexes, logs and storage margin.

Measure the actual footprint and consider storage endurance for continuously writing workloads.

6. Specify Outage Behavior Explicitly

Define which functions must continue when the uplink becomes unavailable.

These may include acquisition, local visualization, approved rule evaluation and historical recording.

Notification delivery is a separate dependency. Local alarm detection can continue while an email or push channel is unavailable.

For buffering, specify:

  • When records become durable.
  • What acknowledgement permits deletion.
  • How repeated deliveries are recognized.
  • Maximum storage consumption.
  • Overflow behavior.
  • Replay rate limits.

Make data loss and queue health visible.

Also define how replay affects rules. Historical observations should not automatically create new live notifications without a documented policy.

7. Treat Updates as Versioned Changes

An application release can change interfaces, mappings, rules and persistent data.

Before deployment, establish:

  1. Supported starting versions.
  2. Configuration compatibility.
  3. Migration requirements.
  4. Backup procedure.
  5. Activation checks.
  6. Rollback conditions.

Start with a representative node or limited deployment group.

After activation, verify acquisition, local access, rules and upstream integration. A running process is only one health signal.

Check Rollback Compatibility

Restoring an older application package may not reverse a data migration.

Confirm whether the previous version can read the resulting configuration and storage format.

Test rollback using realistic runtime data rather than an empty installation.

8. Compare Desired and Reported State

A deployment request does not prove that a node activated the release.

Track intended and reported versions separately:

{
  "nodeId": "edge-014",
  "desiredApplicationVersion": "1.8.0",
  "reportedApplicationVersion": "1.7.3",
  "desiredConfigurationVersion": 12,
  "reportedConfigurationVersion": 11,
  "lastReportedAt": "2026-11-18T08:30:00Z",
  "deploymentStatus": "pending"
}

This is an illustrative record.

Keep report freshness visible. An offline node cannot confirm its current state.

Define how permitted local changes are recorded and reconciled. Otherwise, sites can gradually diverge from the approved deployment without a clear explanation.

9. Build on a Reusable Runtime

Teams can assemble edge applications from separate acquisition, storage, visualization and integration components.

A runtime that combines several responsibilities can reduce the number of independently maintained parts.

Iotellect Edge provides a low-code industrial application runtime for equipment connectivity, local logic, HMI, alarms, history and upstream integration.

The deployment team still needs validated profiles, appropriate hardware, site configuration and tested update procedures.

Document which capabilities are provided by the runtime and which depend on the deployment tooling or project-specific implementation.

Commissioning Checks for Every Installation

Use a repeatable acceptance process.

Verify that:

  • The node has a unique identity and appropriate credentials.
  • Equipment mappings match the installation.
  • Units, scaling and timestamps are correct.
  • Missing and stale data remain distinguishable.
  • Approved rules behave as expected.
  • Required local functions survive an uplink interruption.
  • Buffered data recovers according to policy.
  • Disk limits and queue health are visible.
  • Active application and configuration versions are recorded.
  • Backup and rollback procedures work.

Record exceptions before accepting the site.

A local adjustment that is necessary for operation should become an approved configuration difference or a tracked application change.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can one edge application serve different sites?

Yes, when site differences are represented through supported profiles and validated configuration. Hardware and operating requirements still need testing.

Should credentials be included in a reusable template?

Do not clone node credentials as part of a general application template. Provision identity and access for each installation.

Does local execution guarantee offline operation?

event_model_payload.summary:
An industrial edge pilot can work perfectly while remaining difficult to reproduce.

The engineer knows which register requires scaling, which alarm is disabled and where the site-specific settings live. Deploying the same application elsewhere requires reconstructing those decisions.

A repeatable industrial edge deployment separates application logic from site configuration, node identity and runtime data. It also defines how each installation is validated, updated and recovered.

This guide explains the architecture and deployment practices behind that separation.

1. Define What Runs on the Node

An edge application may handle equipment acquisition, protocol conversion, local rules, operator screens, historical storage and upstream integration.

Document which functions belong locally and which depend on central services.

For each function, identify:

  • Required inputs.
  • External dependencies.
  • Expected behavior during disconnection.
  • Recovery behavior.
  • Resource requirements.

A local dashboard can still depend on remote authentication. A rule can still require a central API. Hosting software on site does not remove those dependencies automatically.

Keep safety functions and time-critical control within their engineered and validated implementations.

For background on acquisition, supervisory functions and deployment boundaries, see Iotellect’s SCADA architecture guide.

2. Separate the Deployment into Four Parts

Avoid copying an entire working installation to create another node.

Separate:

Application release: Reusable rules, screens, mappings and integration logic.

Site configuration: Equipment addresses, asset relationships and approved operating parameters.

Node identity and credentials: Unique identifiers and authorized connections.

Runtime data: History, events, operator actions and queued observations.

These categories need different handling.

An application update should not overwrite local history. A new installation should not inherit another node’s credentials. A rollback must account for persistent data and configuration compatibility.

3. Validate Site Configuration before Activation

Represent site differences as configuration rather than editing application logic at every location.

An illustrative configuration might look like this:

siteId: pumping-station-014
applicationVersion: 1.8.0
configurationVersion: 12

equipment:
  - assetId: pump-01
    deviceProfile: drive-profile-v3
    connection:
      protocol: modbus_tcp
      host: 192.0.2.10
      port: 502
      unitId: 1

telemetry:
  acquisitionIntervalMs: 2000
  staleAfterMs: 10000

storage:
  maximumQueueBytes: 4000000000

This is an application example, not an Iotellect configuration format.

Validation should check required fields, allowed values, supported device profiles and application compatibility.

A simplified validator could include:

def validate_config(config, release):
    require_nonempty(config.site_id)

    if config.application_version != release.version:
        raise ConfigurationError("Application version mismatch")

    if config.telemetry.stale_after_ms <= 0:
        raise ConfigurationError("Invalid freshness policy")

    for asset in config.equipment:
        if asset.device_profile not in release.supported_profiles:
            raise ConfigurationError("Unsupported device profile")

    return config

Production validation also needs schema checks, permitted operating ranges and appropriate error reporting.

Keep secrets out of ordinary exports. Use references to an appropriate credential-management mechanism.

4. Use Device Profiles to Normalize Equipment

Different equipment can expose the same operational concept through different representations.

One drive may report temperature as an integer requiring scaling. Another may expose a floating-point value.

A profile can map both into a shared measurement:

Source address
→ Data type
→ Scaling
→ Engineering unit
→ Application measurement

Document each profile’s:

  • Supported equipment and revisions.
  • Acquisition behavior.
  • Status mappings.
  • Timestamp origin.
  • Quality handling.
  • Available commands.
  • Confirmation method.

Test profiles against representative equipment. Protocol compatibility alone does not establish that the mapping is correct.

Preserve Observation Context

An application record might contain:

{
  "siteId": "pumping-station-014",
  "assetId": "pump-01",
  "measurement": "motor_temperature",
  "value": 61.7,
  "unit": "degC",
  "sourceTimestamp": "2026-11-18T08:30:00Z",
  "quality": "good",
  "profileVersion": "drive-profile-v3"
}

Preserve acquisition time separately from arrival time. An older observation may belong in history without replacing newer current state.

For platform-specific background, see the documentation on Data Table Timestamps and Quality.

5. Size Hardware against a Representative Workload

Tag count alone is insufficient for sizing an edge node.

Resource consumption also depends on acquisition frequency, protocol behavior, storage, calculations, operator sessions and recovery traffic.

Measure:

  • CPU and memory during normal operation.
  • Storage growth.
  • Dashboard response.
  • Queue growth during an outage.
  • Resource use during replay.
  • Application startup and recovery time.

Estimate raw storage using:

records per second
× average record size
× retention duration

For 50 records per second averaging 200 bytes:

50 × 200 × 86,400
= 864,000,000 bytes per day

That is approximately 864 MB per day, before indexes, logs and storage margin.

Measure the actual footprint and consider storage endurance for continuously writing workloads.

6. Specify Outage Behavior Explicitly

Define which functions must continue when the uplink becomes unavailable.

These may include acquisition, local visualization, approved rule evaluation and historical recording.

Notification delivery is a separate dependency. Local alarm detection can continue while an email or push channel is unavailable.

For buffering, specify:

  • When records become durable.
  • What acknowledgement permits deletion.
  • How repeated deliveries are recognized.
  • Maximum storage consumption.
  • Overflow behavior.
  • Replay rate limits.

Make data loss and queue health visible.

Also define how replay affects rules. Historical observations should not automatically create new live notifications without a documented policy.

7. Treat Updates as Versioned Changes

An application release can change interfaces, mappings, rules and persistent data.

Before deployment, establish:

  1. Supported starting versions.
  2. Configuration compatibility.
  3. Migration requirements.
  4. Backup procedure.
  5. Activation checks.
  6. Rollback conditions.

Start with a representative node or limited deployment group.

After activation, verify acquisition, local access, rules and upstream integration. A running process is only one health signal.

Check Rollback Compatibility

Restoring an older application package may not reverse a data migration.

Confirm whether the previous version can read the resulting configuration and storage format.

Test rollback using realistic runtime data rather than an empty installation.

8. Compare Desired and Reported State

A deployment request does not prove that a node activated the release.

Track intended and reported versions separately:

{
  "nodeId": "edge-014",
  "desiredApplicationVersion": "1.8.0",
  "reportedApplicationVersion": "1.7.3",
  "desiredConfigurationVersion": 12,
  "reportedConfigurationVersion": 11,
  "lastReportedAt": "2026-11-18T08:30:00Z",
  "deploymentStatus": "pending"
}

This is an illustrative record.

Keep report freshness visible. An offline node cannot confirm its current state.

Define how permitted local changes are recorded and reconciled. Otherwise, sites can gradually diverge from the approved deployment without a clear explanation.

9. Build on a Reusable Runtime

Teams can assemble edge applications from separate acquisition, storage, visualization and integration components.

A runtime that combines several responsibilities can reduce the number of independently maintained parts.

The deployment team still needs validated profiles, appropriate hardware, site configuration and tested update procedures.

Document which capabilities are provided by the runtime and which depend on the deployment tooling or project-specific implementation.

Use a repeatable acceptance process.

  • The node has a unique identity and appropriate credentials.
  • Equipment mappings match the installation.
  • Units, scaling and timestamps are correct.
  • Missing and stale data remain distinguishable.
  • Approved rules behave as expected.
  • Required local functions survive an uplink interruption.
  • Buffered data recovers according to policy.
  • Disk limits and queue health are visible.
  • Active application and configuration versions are recorded.
  • Backup and rollback procedures work.

Record exceptions before accepting the site.

A local adjustment that is necessary for operation should become an approved configuration difference or a tracked application change.

Frequently Asked Questions

Yes, when site differences are represented through supported profiles and validated configuration. Hardware and operating requirements still need testing.

Should credentials be included in a reusable template?

Do not clone node credentials as part of a general application template. Provision identity and access for each installation.

Does local execution guarantee offline operation?

No. Required dependencies must also be available locally, and the node needs adequate resources and uptime.

What should a pilot prove before expansion?

It should demonstrate repeatable installation, configuration, normal operation, outage handling, updates and recovery.

title: Top Automation Testing Courses for Senior Testers Moving Into Test Lead Roles: Projects, Frameworks and Class Format
summary:
Senior testers preparing for test lead roles should choose automation testing courses that teach framework architecture, real-world project execution, CI/CD integration, and test strategy—not just scripting. Five options worth comparing are Simplilearn, StarAgile, Rahul Shetty Academy, KnowledgeHut, and Test Automation University. Simplilearn and StarAgile offer structured live training, Rahul Shetty Academy emphasizes technical depth, KnowledgeHut focuses on Agile automation strategy, and Test Automation University provides flexible self-paced learning.

The right course depends on your current automation experience, preferred class format, and readiness to manage quality across a team.

Why Senior Testers Need Advanced Automation Testing Skills

Moving from senior software tester to test lead involves more than learning Selenium or creating automated test scripts.

A senior tester typically executes test cases, identifies defects, maintains test scripts, and contributes to release quality. A test lead must also decide what to automate, establish framework standards, assign responsibilities, and communicate testing risks.

The most valuable automation testing courses for experienced professionals should develop five capabilities:

  • Framework architecture: Designing reusable, scalable, and maintainable automation solutions.
  • Automation strategy: Selecting appropriate tests based on business risk, execution frequency, and maintenance costs.
  • CI/CD integration: Connecting automated regression suites with development pipelines.
  • Project leadership: Reviewing automation code, mentoring junior testers, and coordinating testing activities.
  • Quality reporting: Measuring test reliability, coverage, execution performance, and defect trends.

A course that combines technical implementation with these responsibilities provides a stronger foundation for test leadership.

Top 5 Automation Testing Courses for Senior Testers

1. Simplilearn – Automation Testing Master's Program

Best for: Senior testers seeking comprehensive automation engineering training.

Simplilearn offers an automation testing program covering functional testing, API testing, performance testing, and AI-assisted testing. Its structured curriculum makes it suitable for experienced testers who want exposure to multiple automation technologies before assuming broader technical responsibilities.

Projects: The program includes practical assignments and capstone projects involving e-commerce, healthcare, and airline-booking applications. Learners work on functional automation and related testing workflows.

Frameworks: Topics include Selenium, Java, TestNG, Maven, REST Assured, Postman, JMeter, and Playwright-related learning modules.

Class format: Live online instructor-led sessions are combined with self-paced material, giving working professionals opportunities for structured learning and independent practice.

Test lead relevance: The broad curriculum helps learners understand how different testing approaches fit into an overall quality strategy.

Consideration: Senior testers should confirm how much training involves framework architecture, code reviews, and test leadership rather than introductory material.

2. StarAgile – Software and Automation Testing Certification Training

Best for: Senior testers seeking hands-on framework development with live instruction.

StarAgile offers software and automation testing training that combines programming, automation frameworks, practical assignments, and capstone projects. Its curriculum is relevant to experienced testers who want to strengthen their technical capabilities before taking responsibility for automation delivery.

Projects: Published examples include flight-booking automation, an e-commerce framework using Selenium and TestNG, and a telecom API automation framework.

Frameworks: The curriculum covers Selenium WebDriver, Java, Maven, TestNG, Page Object Model, Cucumber BDD, Selenium Grid, and REST Assured.

Class format: Live online instructor-led classes are supported by practical assignments, mentoring, and selected self-paced modules.

Test lead relevance: Framework implementation and multi-domain projects provide opportunities to practise automation design and understand testing workflows.

Consideration: Learners should verify whether their selected batch includes advanced architecture reviews, CI/CD implementation, and team-level automation planning.

3. Rahul Shetty Academy – Java SDET Automation Package

Best for: Experienced testers seeking deeper framework engineering skills.

Rahul Shetty Academy provides a Java-focused automation learning package covering web testing, API automation, mobile testing, and framework design. It is particularly relevant to testers who already understand testing fundamentals but need stronger programming and automation architecture knowledge.

Projects: Training includes practical web, API, and mobile automation exercises designed around real-world testing scenarios and reusable implementation patterns.

Frameworks: Key technologies include Selenium WebDriver, Java, TestNG, JUnit, Maven, Cucumber, REST Assured, and Appium.

Class format: The package is self-paced, allowing professionals to follow the learning sequence independently and revisit technical lessons when necessary.

Test lead relevance: Its design-pattern and framework-focused content can help testers establish coding standards and review automation solutions.

Consideration: Learners seeking structured mentoring, live feedback, or dedicated people-management training may require additional resources.

4. KnowledgeHut – Certified Professional Automation Agile Testing

Best for: Senior testers transitioning toward Agile test leadership responsibilities.

KnowledgeHut offers Certified Professional Automation Agile Testing (CP-AAT) training that emphasizes automation planning within Agile delivery. The course is relevant to experienced testers who already possess technical knowledge and want to make better decisions about automation strategy.

Projects: Practical activities include Agile testing case studies, acceptance-test design, BDD exercises, and collaborative problem-solving based on realistic testing situations.

Frameworks: Topics include TDD, ATDD, BDD, Cucumber, Gherkin, Selenium, JUnit, Maven, and Jenkins integration concepts.

Class format: The provider describes a two-day live instructor-led program featuring group activities, interactive discussions, and practical exercises.

Test lead relevance: The focus on testing strategy, risk assessment, and automation decisions closely matches responsibilities associated with test leadership.

Consideration: The short format is better suited to strategic development than building a comprehensive automation framework from scratch.

5. Test Automation University – Advanced Automation Learning Paths

Best for: Senior testers seeking flexible, specialized automation upskilling.

Test Automation University provides free online courses covering software test automation technologies and engineering practices. Its individual courses allow experienced professionals to strengthen specific skills without committing to a longer classroom-based certification program.

Projects: Practical exercises are available through selected courses, including Playwright-based test development, API interaction, test data management, and continuous integration activities.

Frameworks: Learning topics include Selenium, Playwright, API automation, Page Object patterns, CI/CD practices, and visual testing techniques.

Class format: Courses are self-paced, enabling learners to study independently and select modules according to existing knowledge and professional requirements.

Test lead relevance: Specialized courses can help senior testers evaluate modern frameworks and guide technical improvements within their teams.

Consideration: Learners must organize their own learning pathway and independently develop broader leadership and project-management capabilities.

Quick Comparison: Projects, Frameworks and Class Format

Course provider Primary focus Project approach Class format
Simplilearn End-to-end automation engineering Multi-domain capstone projects Live online + self-paced
StarAgile Applied framework development Web, API, and business application projects Live online + supplementary self-study
Rahul Shetty Academy Advanced Java automation Web, API, and mobile framework exercises Self-paced
KnowledgeHut Agile automation strategy Case studies and collaborative exercises Live instructor-led
Test Automation University Specialized technical upskilling Course-specific coding exercises Self-paced

These programs are not identical substitutes. They differ in technical depth, duration, instructor interaction, and leadership-oriented content.

Which Automation Frameworks Should Future Test Leads Master?

Senior testers do not need expertise in every automation tool. However, they should understand how to select and maintain frameworks that align with their organization's applications and development practices.

Selenium with TestNG or JUnit

Selenium remains relevant for automating web application testing. TestNG and JUnit support test organization, assertions, and execution management.

Test leads should understand how to build reusable test components, introduce parallel execution, and reduce maintenance overhead.

Playwright

Playwright supports modern browser automation and can be used with programming languages including JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, Python, and .NET.

It is useful for teams developing modern web applications that need reliable browser testing and integration with automated delivery pipelines.

Cucumber and BDD

Cucumber enables teams to describe expected application behavior using structured scenarios.

For test leads, the objective is not simply writing Gherkin files. It is improving communication between testers, developers, product owners, and business stakeholders.

REST Assured and API Automation

API testing helps identify defects before they appear in end-to-end user workflows.

Test leads should understand API validation, authentication, test data, negative scenarios, and the balance between API and UI coverage.

Jenkins and CI/CD Tools

Automation becomes more valuable when tests execute consistently within delivery pipelines.

A future test lead should be able to establish test execution policies, evaluate failures, and determine which tests belong in pull-request, nightly, and release-validation pipelines.

Three Practical Projects That Prepare Testers for Lead Roles

Course completion alone does not demonstrate readiness to lead testing activities. Senior professionals should develop portfolio projects that reflect architectural and management decisions.

Project 1: Enterprise E-Commerce Automation Framework

Build a reusable framework covering authentication, product search, checkout, and payment-related test scenarios.

Include Page Object components, test data management, parallel execution, reporting, and source control.

Leadership deliverable: Document framework standards, code review rules, and a regression maintenance plan.

Project 2: API Automation and CI/CD Pipeline

Create API tests for customer registration, account updates, authentication, and error handling.

Integrate the suite with Jenkins or another CI/CD platform and configure reports for failed executions.

Leadership deliverable: Define quality gates, execution schedules, and procedures for investigating failed builds.

Project 3: Automation Strategy for an Agile Team

Prepare an automation roadmap for a hypothetical application with limited testing resources.

Identify high-risk workflows, calculate automation priorities, and assign responsibilities across the testing team.

Leadership deliverable: Present an automation strategy containing milestones, estimated effort, maintenance ownership, and measurable outcomes.

These projects demonstrate the ability to plan, implement, and govern automation—not merely execute scripts.

How to Choose the Right Class Format

Live instructor-led courses are useful when learners want scheduled sessions, feedback, discussions, and support while developing automation skills.

Self-paced courses suit senior testers who already possess coding experience and need targeted learning around specific tools or frameworks.

Blended courses combine instructor interaction with independent learning and can work well for professionals balancing work and training.

Before enrolling, ask whether the program provides live code reviews, reusable project repositories, practical assessments, mentor access, and recordings. Confirm the current syllabus, schedule, fees, and exact certification awarded.

How to Measure Readiness for a Test Lead Role

After training, evaluate your progress against five practical outcomes:

  1. Framework ownership: Can you design a maintainable framework and explain its architectural choices?
  2. Test strategy: Can you prioritize automation based on risk, business value, and maintenance effort?
  3. Pipeline integration: Can you explain test failures, configure execution stages, and manage unreliable tests?
  4. Team guidance: Can you review scripts, establish standards, and mentor other testers?
  5. Reporting: Can you communicate release risks and test results clearly to engineering stakeholders?

Strong performance across these areas provides more meaningful evidence of leadership readiness than a certificate alone.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which automation testing course is best for senior testers becoming test leads?

The best choice depends on existing experience. Simplilearn and StarAgile are options for structured, project-based training. Rahul Shetty Academy supports deeper framework engineering, while KnowledgeHut emphasizes Agile automation planning. Test Automation University is useful for independent specialization.

Is Selenium enough to become a test lead?

No. Selenium is valuable for browser automation, but a test lead must also understand API testing, framework maintainability, CI/CD, test strategy, team coordination, and quality reporting.

Do senior testers need coding skills for test lead roles?

Coding proficiency is helpful, especially when reviewing automation frameworks, diagnosing failures, and mentoring automation engineers. The required depth varies by organization and whether the role is primarily technical or managerial.

Are live classes better than recorded automation testing courses?

Live classes can provide immediate feedback and structured accountability. Recorded courses offer flexibility and repeated access to technical material. Neither is automatically superior; project quality and practical application matter more.

Can automation testing certification guarantee a promotion?

No. Certification demonstrates learning but does not guarantee advancement. Employers also evaluate technical judgment, project ownership, communication skills, mentoring capability, and delivery experience.

Final Thoughts

The best automation testing courses for senior testers moving into test lead roles are those that develop both technical and decision-making skills.

Simplilearn, StarAgile, Rahul Shetty Academy, KnowledgeHut, and Test Automation University offer different learning approaches. Choose according to the gaps in your existing skills rather than provider popularity alone.

Ultimately, test leadership is about building reliable quality processes, guiding teams, and making informed automation decisions. A strong course provides the foundation, while practical project ownership turns those skills into leadership capability.

title: Network Security Basics Every Developer Should Know
summary:
Most developers spend their time on code, but a weak network can undo all of that work. A leaked port, an unpatched router, or a shared Wi-Fi password can give someone a way in, no matter how clean your app is.

Here are the network security basics every developer should have covered. At ZIA Networks, these are the first things we look at when reviewing a setup.

1. Know what is exposed

You can't protect what you can't see. On a network or machine you own, check which ports are open:

nmap -sV your-server-ip

Only scan systems you own or have written permission to test. If you see a port open and you don't know why, that's your first thing to investigate.

2. Close everything you don't need

Default deny is a good rule. Allow only the traffic you actually use. On a Linux server with ufw:

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable

Check the result with:

sudo ufw status verbose

3. Lock down SSH

SSH is one of the most attacked services on the internet. A few small changes help a lot. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config:

PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no

Use key-based login instead of passwords, then restart the service:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

Make sure your key login works in a second terminal before you close your current session, so you don't lock yourself out.

4. Keep everything updated

Operating systems, routers, firewalls, and packages all need regular updates. Many real attacks use bugs that already have a fix.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

5. Don't trust the network by default

Use HTTPS everywhere, even on internal tools. Keep dev, staging, and production separate, and don't reuse the same credentials across them.

6. Keep secrets out of your code

API keys and passwords don't belong in your repo. Use environment variables or a secrets manager, and rotate keys if one is ever exposed.

7. Log and monitor

If nobody is watching, an attack can run for days. Keep logs, set alerts for unusual logins, and review them regularly.

8. Test your backups

A backup you've never restored is only a hope. Do a test restore from time to time.

Quick checklist

  • [ ] Open ports reviewed
  • [ ] Firewall set to deny by default
  • [ ] SSH uses keys, root login off
  • [ ] Updates applied
  • [ ] Secrets out of the repo
  • [ ] Logs and alerts on
  • [ ] Backup restore tested

Wrapping up

None of this is complicated, but it does need to be done consistently. If you'd rather have an expert look over your setup, ZIA Networks helps businesses build and maintain secure, reliable networks with clear advice and dependable support.

title: Incident note: SMTP 550 5.7.1: Relay access denied – causes & fix
summary:
Read the signal

Start with the exact wording of the error and its timestamp in the log. Then narrow down the cause before changing anything.

550 5.7.1 : Relay access denied

Narrow down possible causes

  • The mail client or application sends without SMTP AUTH.
  • Mail is submitted on port 25 instead of submission port 587 (or 465) with login.
  • The recipient domain is missing from virtual_mailbox_domains, mydestination or relay_domains.
  • The application server's IP is not in mynetworks.

Check before changing anything

1.

Show Postfix relay settings

postconf -n | grep -E 'mynetworks|relay_domains|smtpd_relay_restrictions|virtual_mailbox_domains'

2.

Find rejected attempts and client IPs in the log

journalctl -u postfix --since '1 hour ago' | grep 'Relay access denied'

3.

Test authenticated submission on port 587 (prompts for the password)

swaks --to test@example.com --from info@example.com --server mail.example.com --port 587 --tls --auth LOGIN --auth-user info@example.com

4.

Check that the submission ports are listening

ss -ltnp | grep -E ':(25|465|587) '

Fix and test again

  1. Enable SMTP AUTH in the client and use port 587 with STARTTLS.
  2. Add your domains to virtual_mailbox_domains or relay_domains, then run postfix reload.
  3. Set clean relay rules: smtpd_relay_restrictions = permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, defer_unauth_destination.
  4. Add fixed internal servers to mynetworks as single /32 entries – never whole networks.

Then repeat the original action and compare the result with the initial error.

Keep a note for the next ticket

Record the exact error, the check result, the change and the retest. That gives the team a useful starting point next time.

Does 550 5.7.1 always mean relay access denied?

No. 5.7.1 is a generic policy code. Microsoft 365, spam filters and sender restrictions use it too. The text after the code tells you what actually happened.

title: Fixing Silent Misconfigurations in GitLab Runner: Adding Concurrency Alias Support
summary:
When operating self-hosted or cloud infrastructure for CI/CD pipelines, one subtle configuration mistake can cause unexpected resource exhaustion or build instability.

In my recent contribution to GitLab Runner (MR !7782), I solved a long-standing developer trap related to TOML configuration parsing that previously led to runners processing unlimited parallel jobs unintentionally.

Here is the story of how a small alias mapping prevents critical operational failures in production CI/CD environments.

The Problem: The "Concurrency" Trap

GitLab CI/CD documentation and community discussions frequently use the word "concurrency" to describe how many jobs a runner or worker pool can execute simultaneously. Furthermore, within a runner's specific configuration, settings like request_concurrency already use that exact terminology.

Consequently, DevOps engineers and system administrators frequently wrote:

concurrent = 1

[[runners]]
  name = "docker-runner"
  url = "https://gitlab.com"
  concurrency = 1  # ⚠️ Expected: Only run 1 job at a time
  executor = "docker"

Or at the global level:

concurrency = 4    # ⚠️ Expected: Maximum 4 global concurrent jobs

What actually happened?

Under the hood, GitLab Runner uses BurntSushi/toml to unmarshal config.toml into Go structs. Because Go struct tags strictly mapped:

  • concurrent to global Config.Concurrent
  • limit to runner-level RunnerConfig.Limit

Any key named concurrency was silently ignored without raising an error or warning!

Because limit defaulted to its zero value (0), and 0 in GitLab Runner represents unlimited, a runner meant to strictly execute one build at a time would suddenly pick up and run dozens of jobs in parallel. This often resulted in Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, CPU throttling, and failed deployments.

The Solution: Intelligent Alias Fallback

In Merge Request !7782, we implemented alias handling during configuration loading:

  1. Global Level: If concurrent is not set but concurrency is present in the configuration, concurrency is mapped directly to Config.Concurrent.
  2. Runner Level ([[runners]]): If limit is not explicitly set, concurrency is mapped directly to RunnerConfig.Limit.
  3. 100% Backward Compatibility: Canonical keys (concurrent and limit) take priority if both are specified, ensuring existing configurations remain unaffected. 
# Now fully supported and safe!
concurrency = 4

[[runners]]
  name = "production-runner"
  url = "https://gitlab.com"
  concurrency = 1   # Enforces single-job execution as expected
  executor = "docker"

Verifying with Table-Driven Tests in Go

To ensure this fallback works reliably across all combinations of configurations, we added comprehensive table-driven tests (TestLoadConfig_ConcurrencyAlias):

  • Scenario A: Only concurrency specified at root level → Maps to Concurrent.
  • Scenario B: Only concurrency specified in [[runners]] → Maps to Limit.
  • Scenario C: Both concurrent/limit and concurrency present → Canonical fields take precedence.
  • Scenario D: Unset values retain their standard defaults. 
go test -v ./common -run '^TestLoadConfig_ConcurrencyAlias$'

All test cases pass cleanly, safeguarding runner stability across minor and major upgrades.

Key Takeaways

  1. Developer UX matters in Infra Configs: If operators commonly guess a configuration key based on natural naming conventions or documentation phrasing, supporting it as an alias eliminates dangerous failure modes.
  2. Beware of Silent Unmarshaling: When unmarshaling TOML/YAML/JSON in Go, unused fields don't always produce syntax errors, which can leave critical limits at their uninitialized zero values.
  3. Open Source Contribution: Small, well-targeted improvements can resolve issues open for years (Issue #4793) and prevent real-world production outages.

Check out the merged implementation on GitLab:
